scenes.heading: Le Chatelier’s principle
scenes.sub: What does an equilibrium do when you push it?
scenes.say: Once a reaction reaches equilibrium, it doesn't stay put when you change the conditions. Le Chatelier's principle lets you predict which way it will shift.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: A group boards the front of a train; people shuffle to the back
scenes.science: Add a reactant and the equilibrium shifts right, using some up
scenes.breaks: people choose to move, but an equilibrium shifts because extra particles collide more often, until Q equals K again.
scenes.say: Picture a crowded train. A group gets on at the front, so people shuffle towards the back. The front ends up less crowded than right after they boarded, but still more than before. Add a reactant, and an equilibrium shifts right, using up some, but not all, of it.

scenes.heading: The principle
points: A disturbed equilibrium partially opposes the change
Check with Q: Q < K right, Q > K left
scenes.say: Le Chatelier's principle says a disturbed equilibrium adjusts to partially oppose the change, never fully cancelling it. Shift right means more products; shift left means more reactants. You can check with Q and K.

scenes.heading: Concentration and pressure
points: Add reactant or remove product: shift right
Smaller volume: shift to fewer gas moles
Same gas moles each side: no shift
Inert gas at constant volume: no shift
scenes.say: Add a reactant or remove a product, and it shifts right. Add a product, and it shifts left. Squeeze a gas mixture, and it shifts to fewer gas moles, unless both sides are equal. An inert gas at constant volume causes no shift.

scenes.heading: Raising the temperature
scenes.say: Treat heat like a chemical. For an exothermic reaction, heat is a product, so heating shifts it left and K falls. For an endothermic reaction, heating shifts it right and K rises. Temperature is the only change that alters K.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃, ΔH = −197 kJ mol⁻¹. What happens to the amount of SO₃?
lines: Add O₂: Q < K, shift right, more SO₃
Halve volume: 3 gas mol → 2, shift right
Heat it: exothermic, shift left, less SO₃
scenes.say: Adding oxygen makes Q less than K, so more S O three forms. Halving the volume shifts towards fewer gas moles, three to two, so right again. Heating shifts this exothermic reaction left. Argon at constant volume does nothing.
scenes.caption: Adding O₂ makes Q less than K, so more SO₃ forms. Halving the volume shifts towards fewer gas moles, 3 to 2, so right again. Heating shifts this exothermic reaction left. Argon at constant volume does nothing.

scenes.heading: Haber process compromise
steps: High pressure: more yield and rate
Remove NH₃, recycle N₂ and H₂
scenes.say: In the Haber process, high pressure helps both yield and rate. A low temperature helps yield but is too slow, so a compromise temperature is used. An iron catalyst speeds things up, and ammonia is removed while unreacted gases are recycled.
scenes.caption: In the Haber process, high pressure helps both yield and rate. A low temperature helps yield but is too slow, so a compromise temperature is used. An iron catalyst speeds things up, and NH₃ is removed while unreacted gases are recycled.

points: Smaller volume: shift to fewer gas moles
scenes.say: Quick recap. An equilibrium partially opposes any change. Heating favours the endothermic direction, and only temperature changes K. Catalysts change the rate, never the yield. Now try the practice questions!
